cues.say: Component twenty: the load test and the game day.
Two practices before a launch. A load test fires fake traffic, two to three times the expected peak, at a test copy, against a pass bar. A game day is a rehearsal: flip switches, fake outages.
Tools like k6 or Locust play the fake users.
Why bother? Otherwise you find problems on sale day. At six AM, checkout crawls: a missing index. An index lets the database jump to the rows it needs, instead of reading every row.
Then payments fail, and nobody has practiced pausing orders.
A load test starts with a script of one user: open the deal, add the TV, and pay, with Stripe in test mode. The tool runs thousands at once.
It ramps traffic past the expected peak, to two or three times it, aimed at staging: a test copy, never real customers.
And you write the pass bar first. Zero TVs oversold, zero double charges, and p95 under five hundred milliseconds.
P95 means ninety-five percent of requests are faster than that. It shows the slow tail.
A game day is the rehearsal: flip every switch, fake Stripe errors, check that alerts fire, and time each response.
The load test finds slow queries, missing indexes, and too few copies.
The game day finds switches that don't work, and alerts that don't fire.
Now a real case, two days before a doorbuster sale. k6 simulates a hundred and twenty thousand visitors. A thousand try to buy one TV deal, with fifty in stock.
Run one sells exactly fifty, with no double charges, but fails the p95 bar: a missing index.
Add the index, rerun, and it passes. Found two days early, not at six AM on sale day.
Then the game day: every switch flipped, Stripe errors faked, the response timed.
It sits outside your system, aimed at a full copy of it, with Stripe in test mode.
Two things to know. Size staging like production, or the numbers lie.
And fake traffic is a guess, so model real users: most browse, a few buy.
In the interview, say: pass means zero oversold, zero double charges, and p95 under five hundred milliseconds.
